abstract: # VLADrop: Drop-Then-Recovery (DTR) ### How Redundant Are Vision-Language-Action Models? [ ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27755) [ ](https://huggingface.co/collections/s1ghhh/vladrop-drop-then-recovery-dtr-checkpoints-6a509dd598cf54ae53060204) [ ](https://github.com/s1ghhh/VLADrop) [ ](./LICENSE) 📑 [**Paper**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27755)  |  🤗 [**Checkpoints**](https://huggingface.co/collections/s1ghhh/vladrop-drop-then-recovery-dtr-checkpoints-6a509dd598cf54ae53060204) DTR ranks a pretrained VLA's transformer blocks with GateProbe , physically removes the least important ones, and recovery fine-tunes the smaller model to measure whether the removed capacity was ever necessary for closed-loop control. --- Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models inherit oversized language backbones from pretrained VLMs, whose capacity far exceeds what short robotic instructions require. **Drop-Then-Recovery (DTR)** is an analysis protocol that removes selected transformer blocks from a pretrained VLA and then fine-tunes the result, and **GateProbe** is a one-shot virtual-gate sensitivity metric that ranks blocks by their contribution to the downstream action loss. Across four architectures and three benchmarks we find a strong asymmetry: **language backbones are highly redundant for standard manipulation, while vision and action pathways are not.** ## 🔥 Highlights - **Removing half the language blocks helps, not hurts.** On LIBERO, dropping half of OpenVLA-OFT's LLM blocks *improves* success rate **95.0% → 98.3%** under the same fine-tuning budget, at ~55% of the size and FLOPs. - **Two blocks are enough.** Keeping only 2 language blocks (**16.6% of model size**) still recovers baseline-level performance (95.1% on OpenVLA-OFT, 91.0% on pi0.5). - **The redundancy is asymmetric.** Under the same intervention, dropping *vision* or *action* blocks collapses performance (down to 62.4% / 26.2% on pi0.5), confirming these pathways are far less compressible than language. - **It ge
